page: Vultr vhp-4c-12gb-amd is a High Performance family virtual server configured with 4 shared vCPUs and 12.0 GB of system memory, translating to 3.0 GB of RAM per core. Powered by an AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture, the instance utilizes 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The CPU features a 16 MB L3 cache, 32 KB L1d cache, and 0.5 MB L2 cache, with hardware support for AVX, AES, and SHA_NI cryptographic instructions. Local storage is bundled with a 260 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU accelerators are present.

Benchmark results indicate moderate compute capabilities alongside notable memory and processing bottlenecks. The instance achieves average performance in stress-ng single-core and multi-core tests, as well as in Geekbench single-core execution. However, its shared CPU allocation and memory architecture present performance tradeoffs. Large-block uncached memory read and write bandwidth are weak, registering at 24.31 GB/sec and 20.91 GB/sec respectively, while the Passmark memory score falls into the bottom 10 percent. Furthermore, database operations and bzip3 decompression benchmarks are poor, reflecting resource constraints under sustained, data-intensive workloads.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, this instance offers a high-density storage-to-compute ratio for budget-conscious deployments, leveraging shared AMD EPYC resources to minimize overhead. It is best suited for workloads that do not require sustained, dedicated CPU performance, such as light web serving, basic text processing, or development environments. It is less suitable for high-throughput database operations, intensive software compilation, or heavy data decompression tasks due to the documented performance limitations in those areas.
description: Vultr vhp-4c-12gb-amd is a High Performance virtual server featuring 4 shared AMD EPYC vCPUs, 12.0 GB of RAM, and a 260 GB NVMe SSD. Operating on the x86_64 architecture at 2.0 GHz, this instance includes 2 physical cores with hyper-threading and a 16 MB L3 cache. While it delivers average single-core CPU performance in stress-ng and Geekbench tests, its shared CPU allocation and weak large-block memory bandwidth present clear performance tradeoffs. Benchmarks indicate poor performance in database operations and multi-threaded decompression. Consequently, this server is qualitatively cost-effective for budget-sensitive, low-concurrency workloads like light web serving, text processing, and development environments, rather than resource-intensive database or compilation tasks.
